interview_metadata.name: Antonio Gonzalez
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born in Ponce, Puerto Rico, in 1949, and I came to the mainland with my parents when I was a little boy. We first stayed with relatives in New York, then my father found steadier factory work around Boston, so by the time I was in school I was growing up in a Spanish-speaking house in Massachusetts. My parents were Catholic and strict about manners, work, and family; Three Kings Day, rice on the stove, cousins sleeping over, that was normal life. I finished high school, then went right to work because money was tight and I liked fixing things more than sitting in classrooms. I became a maintenance mechanic in a manufacturing plant, and I stayed in that kind of work for almost forty years, repairing pumps, belts, motors, wiring, anything that kept the line moving. I married my wife Maria when I was in my twenties, and we raised three children. We moved to Taunton later because it was quieter, we could afford a house, and I wanted a garage and a little yard. Retirement has been good, but I keep busy with woodworking, fishing, church, dominoes, my garden, and my grandchildren.

follow_ups.question: What memories from childhood still feel strongest to you?
follow_ups.response: The smell of sofrito and coffee in the morning, my mother telling us to answer adults in Spanish, and my father coming home tired with grease on his hands are the memories that stay with me.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you to fix things?
follow_ups.response: My father started it, then older mechanics at the plant really taught me; they would say, 'Listen to the machine first,' and I still believe that.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The big crossroads was after high school. A cousin wanted me to go with him to New York and try restaurant work, and another friend was talking about the military, but I had been offered an entry job at a plant near Boston. It was not glamorous, sweeping floors and helping the mechanics, but I saw a future there. I chose the plant because it meant a paycheck every week and I could stay close to my parents. That choice made me a steady man. It gave me skills, benefits, a union card later on, and enough stability to marry Maria and buy our house.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone advise you at that time?
follow_ups.response: My father told me, 'A trade feeds a family,' and that settled in my head more than anything else.

follow_ups.question: What do you think would have happened if you had gone to New York?
follow_ups.response: Maybe I would have made more quick money, maybe not, but I do not think I would have built the same steady life.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice, but not the kind where you sit with a notebook and make a big plan. I looked at what was in front of me: family nearby, a real job, and a chance to learn a trade.

follow_ups.question: Were you scared making that choice?
follow_ups.response: A little, yes, because I was young and did not know if the plant would keep me.

follow_ups.question: Did you feel proud afterward?
follow_ups.response: I did, especially when I brought home my first regular paycheck and helped my mother with groceries.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes, I think guidance counselors or apprenticeship programs could have helped me understand options better. Back then nobody explained much to kids like me; you found work through family, neighbors, or luck.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Someone explaining training programs, wages, and how to move up would have saved me some guessing.

follow_ups.question: Do you try to offer that help now?
follow_ups.response: Yes, with my grandchildren I talk plainly about trades, college, debt, and not being ashamed to work with your hands.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: My wife is Maria, and we have been married over fifty years. She is the person who knows all my habits, good and bad, and she keeps the calendar because I start projects and forget what day it is. We have three grown children: Elena in Bridgewater, Miguel in New Bedford, and Carmen here in Taunton. They all have their own busy lives, but we talk every week, and Sunday dinner still brings people over when schedules allow. I have grandchildren, and they are a big reason I keep cooking the old dishes and telling stories in Spanish. Family is not just birthdays for us; it is rides to appointments, fixing a leaky sink, watching a ballgame together, and checking who needs what.

follow_ups.question: Who do you see most often?
follow_ups.response: Carmen is closest, so she stops by once or twice a week, and Elena usually comes on Sundays when she can.

follow_ups.question: What do you and Maria do together day to day?
follow_ups.response: We drink coffee in the morning, go to Mass most Sundays, watch the news, argue gently about the Red Sox, and plan meals around who might visit.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have a younger sister, Isabel, in Rhode Island, and a brother, Rafael, in Florida. We do not see each other every month, but we call and keep up with family news.

follow_ups.question: Who are you closest to among your siblings?
follow_ups.response: Isabel, because she is nearby and remembers the same Boston years I do.

follow_ups.question: Do you have relatives in Puerto Rico?
follow_ups.response: Yes, cousins mostly, and I want to visit them again before traveling gets too hard.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Outside family, my closest people are the men I play dominoes with and a few old coworkers. We meet weekly, usually Thursday afternoon, and it gets loud because nobody likes to lose. I also know people through church, the senior walking group, and the Taunton River Anglers Association. Those friendships matter because after retirement you can get quiet if you do not make yourself show up somewhere.

follow_ups.question: Who is your closest friend right now?
follow_ups.response: A man named Joe Martins, an old plant electrician; we fish together and still talk like we are on break at work.

follow_ups.question: How often do you socialize outside the house?
follow_ups.response: Usually three or four times a week between dominoes, walking, church, fishing, or errands where I run into people.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Taunton, in a working-class neighborhood with older houses, small yards, and people who mostly mind their business but will help if you ask. I like that I can get to the grocery store, church, the river, and the senior center without a big production. You hear lawn mowers, dogs, kids after school, and in the summer I am outside with tomatoes and peppers. It is not fancy, but it feels lived in. There are Portuguese families, Puerto Rican families, Cape Verdean families, Irish old-timers, a good mix.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors well?
follow_ups.response: I know the ones on both sides well enough to share tools, vegetables, and snowblower help.

follow_ups.question: What places nearby are part of your routine?
follow_ups.response: Market Basket, St. Mary's parish, the senior center, the Taunton River spots, and the hardware store are my regular stops.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. We lock doors and keep porch lights on, but I am comfortable walking in daylight and I know who belongs on the street.

follow_ups.question: Are there times you feel less safe?
follow_ups.response: Late at night I do not walk around much, mostly because of traffic and my knees, not because I am scared.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened nearby?
follow_ups.response: There have been car break-ins a couple streets over, so I tell everyone not to leave things visible.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The good part is the space, the community, and being near family. The hard part is winter, property taxes, and watching some houses get neglected when older owners cannot keep up.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you from moving?
follow_ups.response: The house is ours, my shop is in the garage, and Maria has her routines here.

follow_ups.question: What would you change about the area?
follow_ups.response: Better sidewalks and more reliable transportation for seniors would help a lot.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is just me and my wife Maria living in the house. We have the upstairs bedrooms ready because grandchildren sometimes stay over, but nobody else is living here full time. Maria handles more of the bills and appointments, and I do more of the repairs, yard, and cooking when family comes. It is quiet most weekdays, then busier when somebody drops by.

follow_ups.question: How do you divide household chores?
follow_ups.response: I cook the Puerto Rican dishes, garden, fix things, and take trash out; Maria handles laundry, paperwork, and keeping me on schedule.

follow_ups.question: Do grandchildren stay overnight often?
follow_ups.response: Not as often now that they are older, but a grandchild may stay on a weekend or during school vacation.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent; it is just Maria and me.

follow_ups.question: No one staying short-term right now?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, the household has been just the two of us for years.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Grandchildren sometimes stay for a night, and my sister Isabel has stayed after family events.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once every month or two, more around holidays.

follow_ups.question: Where do they sleep?
follow_ups.response: We keep the spare bedroom ready with clean sheets.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody who usually lives here is away.

follow_ups.question: No one away at college?
follow_ups.response: No, the grandchildren live with their parents.

follow_ups.question: No hospital stay right now?
follow_ups.response: No, thank God, not right now.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Most mornings I am up around 6:30, make coffee, check my sugar, and water the garden if it is warm. Monday is usually errands, Tuesday I may go to the senior walking group, Thursday is dominoes, and weekends are for church, family, fishing, or Red Sox games. I do not punch a clock anymore, so I have to make my own structure. Some days I spend three hours in the garage on a bench or shelf and forget lunch until Maria calls me in. Evenings are quieter: dinner, news, maybe a ballgame or music.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 10:30, unless the Red Sox game runs late and is close.

follow_ups.question: What is the most regular appointment in your week?
follow_ups.response: Sunday Mass and Thursday dominoes are the ones I protect the most.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I am retired now, so I do not have a paid job. My old work was maintenance mechanic work in a manufacturing plant, usually day shift but sometimes overtime or emergency calls when equipment broke down. Now my work is unpaid: fixing things at home, helping neighbors with small repairs, and teaching grandkids how to use tools safely. I sometimes joke that retirement gave me a worse boss because Maria's list never ends.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever take paid repair jobs?
follow_ups.response: No formal jobs; if a neighbor insists, they might give me coffee, plant starts, or a gift card.

follow_ups.question: Do you miss paid work?
follow_ups.response: I miss the men and the problem-solving, but I do not miss the noise or the pressure when production stopped.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I manage my medications, help Maria with appointments, keep up with the house, and check on a couple older neighbors after storms. In summer the garden becomes a responsibility because tomatoes do not wait for you. I also do genealogy work on the computer a few afternoons a month, scanning old photos and writing names before they disappear from memory.

follow_ups.question: What medications are part of your routine?
follow_ups.response: Blood pressure medicine, diabetes medicine, a cholesterol pill, and sometimes acetaminophen for arthritis pain.

follow_ups.question: Who relies on you outside your home?
follow_ups.response: My next-door neighbor asks me about small repairs, and my children call when something breaks or they need advice.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest change is I walk more deliberately now because my knees complain if I skip it. I joined the seniors' walking group, and that gave me a set time instead of saying I will exercise later. I also spend more time on video calls with family than I used to. Since the pandemic years, we got used to using the tablet for birthdays and check-ins with relatives far away.

follow_ups.question: When did you join the walking group?
follow_ups.response: About a year and a half ago, after my doctor told me my sugar numbers would improve if I moved more.

follow_ups.question: Has the computer become easier for you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, basic things like email, video calls, and family history websites are easier, though passwords still annoy me.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: My children are grown, so I can only talk about when they were young. Back then I left early for the plant, Maria got them ready for school, and afternoons were homework, chores, church activities, baseball, or music depending on the child. Now with the grandchildren, I hear about soccer, part-time jobs, school clubs, and too much time on phones. I help with rides sometimes, but I am not the main scheduler.

follow_ups.question: Which grandchild do you help most with rides?
follow_ups.response: Carmen's youngest, Mateo, because they are here in Taunton.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with homework?
follow_ups.response: Mostly history projects or family tree assignments; for new math, I send them to their parents.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Personally, I have had small experiences: traffic stops, reporting a stolen tool once, and seeing police around the neighborhood. As a Puerto Rican young man in Boston years ago, I learned to be polite and careful because some officers looked at you like you were trouble before you opened your mouth. I was never arrested, but I remember being stopped with friends and asked where we were going when we were just walking home. Those things stay with you.

follow_ups.question: When did that stop with friends happen?
follow_ups.response: Late 1960s, in Boston, when we were teenagers or just out of school.

follow_ups.question: How do you act during a traffic stop now?
follow_ups.response: Hands visible, yes sir, no arguing on the roadside; that is what I taught my sons too.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: A good experience was when an officer helped after Maria had a fender bender years ago. A bad memory is police treating a group of Latino boys as suspicious just for standing near a corner store.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever file a complaint?
follow_ups.response: No, back then we did not think anyone would listen.

follow_ups.question: Do you know local officers now?
follow_ups.response: Only casually from community events and traffic details near church.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. I had one nephew who got in trouble for a DUI years ago, and the family was angry but also helped him get straightened out.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect your family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it scared everyone because he could have hurt somebody, and my sister made sure he took it seriously.

follow_ups.question: Any other close arrests?
follow_ups.response: No close family beyond that.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote almost every time, especially presidential, state, and local elections. My parents could not always speak English confidently, so when I became old enough, voting felt like speaking up for the family. Maria and I usually go together or vote by mail if the weather is bad. I may not follow every political fight, but I believe you cannot complain and then stay home.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote in local elections too?
follow_ups.response: Yes, though I admit I have missed a small special election here or there.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide on local candidates?
follow_ups.response: I read the local paper, listen at the senior center, and look for who understands roads, taxes, schools, and seniors.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would say I am a moderate Democrat, maybe old-fashioned in some ways. I believe in working, paying your way, respecting family, and not wasting money, but I also believe government has a job when people are old, sick, poor, or treated unfairly. Social Security, Medicare, unions, public schools, those things mattered in my life. I am Catholic, so I think about dignity and helping people, but I do not like politicians using religion just to win votes. I am not far left, and I am not comfortable with cruelty toward immigrants or people who are struggling. I care about taxes because I own a home, but I also know good services cost money.

follow_ups.question: What issues matter most to you?
follow_ups.response: Health care, Social Security, cost of living, fair treatment for working people, and whether my grandchildren can afford a decent life.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics with friends?
follow_ups.response: A little at dominoes, but we keep it from ruining the game because some men get heated.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more worried about how angry politics has gotten. Years ago people disagreed, but now families can stop talking over it. I also pay more attention to health care and senior costs than I did when I was working. My basic views did not change completely; I still lean Democratic and pro-labor. But I am less patient with politicians who make noise and do not fix anything practical.

follow_ups.question: Did the pandemic change your views?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it made me value public health workers more and made me impatient with people spreading nonsense.

follow_ups.question: Have any family members shifted politically?
follow_ups.response: Some younger relatives are more progressive than me, especially on climate and policing.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: It affected me somewhat to a lot. I am not Black, but as a Puerto Rican man I know what it feels like to be judged by accent, skin tone, or neighborhood. Watching those videos of police violence was painful, and it made me think about stories from when I was young. I also listened to my grandchildren, because they speak about race more openly than my generation did. I support accountability, and I also want safe neighborhoods, so to me it cannot be slogans only.

follow_ups.question: Did you attend any protests?
follow_ups.response: No, with my knees and age I did not march, but I followed closely and talked with family.

follow_ups.question: What did your grandchildren say?
follow_ups.response: They talked about school discussions, bias, and wanting police to be trained and held responsible.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the movement raises real issues: unequal treatment, fear during police stops, and whether people believe complaints from minority communities. I also think regular people sometimes talk past each other because one side hears 'anti-police' and the other hears 'you do not care if people die.' My view is that good policing and accountability go together. In a plant, if a mechanic made dangerous mistakes, you corrected it; you did not hide it to protect the department.

follow_ups.question: Do you think reforms are needed locally?
follow_ups.response: Yes, training, body cameras where appropriate, community relationships, and clear discipline rules are reasonable.

follow_ups.question: Do your friends agree?
follow_ups.response: Some do, some think the topic is exaggerated, and then the domino table gets quiet.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think the country is still learning how to tell the truth about itself. My family came from Puerto Rico and worked hard, but hard work did not erase discrimination or language barriers. I see young people naming things we used to swallow silently. At the same time, I want conversations that leave room for people to learn, because if everyone is only accused, they shut down. Race is not just Black and white; Latino people carry many colors and histories too.

follow_ups.question: How do you describe your own racial identity?
follow_ups.response: I say Hispanic or Puerto Rican first, and racially I usually mark White or multiracial because our family has Spanish, Taino, and Afro-Caribbean roots.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about this with family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially with grandchildren when they ask about what it was like for me growing up.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I mostly talked with family and close friends. I did not join protests, but I watched, read, and tried not to dismiss what younger people were saying.

follow_ups.question: Where did those conversations happen?
follow_ups.response: Mostly Sunday dinner, phone calls, and once after Mass in the parking lot.

follow_ups.question: Did you change any behavior?
follow_ups.response: I became more careful about listening first before saying, 'In my day,' because that phrase can close ears.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My children are sympathetic to the issues but practical, like me. The grandchildren are more outspoken, especially online and at school. Some older friends think the movement went too far, and others say it was overdue. Maria mostly says we should pray, listen, and treat people with dignity, which sounds simple but is not always followed.

follow_ups.question: Any conflict in the family over it?
follow_ups.response: Small disagreements, but nothing that broke relationships.

follow_ups.question: Who influenced your thinking most?
follow_ups.response: My grandchildren, because they asked direct questions and expected honest answers.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: For seventy-seven, I am doing all right, but I have things to manage. I have high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, cholesterol medicine, arthritis in my knees and hands, and some lower back pain from years of plant work. I use hearing aids sometimes, especially in groups. My doctor wants me walking, eating smaller portions, and keeping up with appointments. I still fish, garden, and work in the garage, just slower and with more breaks.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your doctor?
follow_ups.response: My primary doctor about every three or four months for diabetes and blood pressure checks.

follow_ups.question: What limits you most?
follow_ups.response: The knees, especially stairs, long walks, and standing too long at the workbench.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: What makes it easy is Maria helping with meals, Medicare coverage, and having places to walk. What makes it hard is loving rice, plantains, bread, and big family plates. Arthritis also makes exercise less automatic. I have learned not to pretend I am forty; I do smaller portions and keep moving.

follow_ups.question: What food is hardest to limit?
follow_ups.response: Arroz con gandules and fried plantains, no question.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit actually works for you?
follow_ups.response: Walking with other seniors works because someone notices if I do not show up.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: In the past two years, the main thing was my A1C creeping up, and my doctor got firm with me. We adjusted medicine and I started walking more regularly. I also had a bad knee flare last winter after shoveling too much snow, which was my own fault. No broken bones, thank God, and I had cataract surgery a few years back that went well.

follow_ups.question: Did the diabetes change your daily routine?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I check sugar more regularly and try not to eat late-night sweets during ballgames.

follow_ups.question: Did you need physical therapy for the knee?
follow_ups.response: A few sessions and exercises at home, though I do not do them as faithfully as Maria wants.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Since I am retired, it does not affect paid work, but it affects how much I can do in a day. I pace myself with repairs and avoid ladders unless one of my sons is there.

follow_ups.question: Have you stopped doing any tasks?
follow_ups.response: I stopped getting on the roof and I do not move heavy appliances anymore.

follow_ups.question: Does that bother you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because I like being useful, but I would rather ask for help than fall.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Maria has arthritis and thyroid issues, and she had a scare with her heart rhythm a while back. That made me nervous because she is the center of the house. I also worry about my sister's diabetes and about older cousins in Puerto Rico who do not always get appointments quickly. In our family, someone's health problem becomes everyone's schedule problem.

follow_ups.question: Do you go with Maria to appointments?
follow_ups.response: Yes, for bigger appointments I drive and sit with her so we both hear the instructions.

follow_ups.question: Who helps you when you need support?
follow_ups.response: Carmen is closest, and Miguel will come quickly for heavier things.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We are fortunate to have Medicare and supplemental coverage, but health care is still paperwork, phone menus, referrals, and waiting. I have not completely forgone care, but I have delayed dental work because the cost was irritating and not covered the same way. Maria had to wait longer than we liked for a specialist appointment. The doctors are mostly good; the system is the tiring part.

follow_ups.question: What is hardest to navigate?
follow_ups.response: Insurance statements and figuring out what is covered before the bill arrives.

follow_ups.question: Do language barriers affect you now?
follow_ups.response: Not for me, but I still translate for older relatives who are more comfortable in Spanish.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Yes, in the informal family way. My mother used teas, Vicks, soups, prayer, and advice from older women in the family. We still use ginger tea, honey, warm compresses, and certain herbs for comfort, but I do not replace the doctor with that. If my blood pressure is high, I take the medicine. The old remedies are for soothing, not pretending diabetes disappears.

follow_ups.question: Any specific remedy you still use?
follow_ups.response: Ginger tea with a little honey for a cold, and warm salt water gargle.

follow_ups.question: Does faith play into healing?
follow_ups.response: Yes, prayer helps calm us, but I believe God also gave us doctors.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I smoked when I was young, especially during plant breaks, but I quit in the late 1980s after coughing too much and Maria getting on me. I drink lightly now, maybe a beer at a cookout or a small rum drink at Christmas, not as coping. When I am stressed I go to the garage, put on salsa, or sharpen tools. Smoking is behind me.

follow_ups.question: How did you quit smoking?
follow_ups.response: Mostly stubbornness, Maria's pressure, and seeing older coworkers with breathing problems.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep alcohol in the house?
follow_ups.response: A little for holidays or guests, but it is not an everyday thing.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I take prescribed medications for blood pressure, diabetes, and cholesterol, and I take over-the-counter pain reliever when arthritis is bad. I do not use marijuana or other substances. The most recent pain medicine was acetaminophen after I spent too long sanding a bench and my hands stiffened up. I am careful because I know some medicines can cause trouble if you mix them or take too much.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever use stronger pain pills?
follow_ups.response: No, not currently; after dental work years ago I had a prescription, but I did not like feeling foggy.

follow_ups.question: Who manages the pill schedule?
follow_ups.response: I fill my weekly pill box, and Maria double-checks if I am distracted.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: Medicare, our supplemental plan, and my pension income keep it manageable. We budget for copays, prescriptions, glasses, and dental because those surprises can bite you. Our children would help in an emergency, but we try not to lean on them. I keep a folder with appointments and bills because if you do not track it, the paperwork multiplies.

follow_ups.question: Are prescriptions affordable?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, though every January I check prices and complain a little.

follow_ups.question: Do you use one pharmacy?
follow_ups.response: Yes, the same local pharmacy because they know us and catch questions.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am pro-vaccine. Maria and I got COVID shots and boosters, flu shots, shingles shots, whatever the doctor recommends for our age.

follow_ups.question: Were you hesitant at first?
follow_ups.response: I had questions, but I was not against it; I asked my doctor and pharmacist.

follow_ups.question: Do you encourage family to vaccinate?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially around babies, older people, and anyone with health problems.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: My primary doctor, the pharmacist, Medicare notices, and public health information from Massachusetts are what I trust. I do not take medical advice from Facebook arguments. My daughter Elena is good at looking up reliable sources and explaining them without drama. If something sounds too exciting or too frightening, I wait before believing it.

follow_ups.question: Do you watch TV news for health information?
follow_ups.response: Some, but I still verify with the doctor because TV can make everything sound urgent.

follow_ups.question: Do you read Spanish-language health information?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes for relatives, but I prefer official sources or clinic handouts.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Overall I have been grateful, but not carefree. Aging brings a little grief because friends get sick, people you worked with die, and your body reminds you every morning that time passed. I have good days when the garden is growing and the grandkids visit, and I have quiet days when I feel useless if I cannot do what I used to. I do not sit and cry, but I do think more about legacy. That is why I am trying to write family stories down.

follow_ups.question: What lifts your mood most?
follow_ups.response: Music in the kitchen, family at the table, catching fish, and finishing a project that comes out square.

follow_ups.question: What brings your mood down?
follow_ups.response: Pain, bad news about friends, and feeling like the world is moving faster than I can follow.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: Last winter an old coworker named Frank passed away. We had not seen each other every week, but we had spent thousands of hours in the same plant noise, and his death hit me. I went into the garage and found a tool he had given me, and suddenly I felt the whole weight of those years. Maria found me sitting there doing nothing, which is not like me. We went to the wake, and afterward I called another old coworker instead of keeping it inside.

follow_ups.question: What helped you through that week?
follow_ups.response: Talking with people who knew him, going to Mass, and making a small wooden cross for my shop shelf.

follow_ups.question: Did it change anything for you?
follow_ups.response: It made me call old friends more often instead of assuming there is always time.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have not been diagnosed with depression or anxiety. I do get worried, especially about health, money surprises, and family, and sometimes I get restless if I have no project. My way is to keep moving, pray, talk to Maria, or go outside. I know men my age sometimes hide feelings too much, so I am trying to be better about saying when something bothers me.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever seen a counselor?
follow_ups.response: No, not for myself, though I would not insult someone else for doing it.

follow_ups.question: How do you know when stress is building?
follow_ups.response: I get short-tempered over little things, like a missing tool or a bill I do not understand.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: The family has had stress, mostly work pressure for the kids and school pressure for the grandchildren. Maria worries about everyone, so I try to keep the house calm when they come over.

follow_ups.question: Who seems most stressed?
follow_ups.response: Carmen, because she balances work, kids, and checking on us.

follow_ups.question: How do you support them?
follow_ups.response: Food, rides, repairs, listening, and sometimes slipping a grandchild gas money.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Religion is important to me. I was raised Catholic, and I still identify as Catholic and attend Mass most Sundays with Maria. I am not the loudest religious person, but the Church shaped my ideas about family, duty, forgiveness, and helping people. We celebrate Christmas, Three Kings Day, Holy Week, and the feast days that connect to Puerto Rican tradition. Prayer is part of my day, especially when someone is sick. I have frustrations with the Church as an institution, but faith itself is still a foundation.

follow_ups.question: What parish do you attend?
follow_ups.response: We usually attend St. Mary's in Taunton, unless we are visiting family.

follow_ups.question: Do you volunteer through church?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I help with setup, small repairs, food drives, or translating informally when needed.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I use Facebook, mostly to see family photos, church notices, Puerto Rican community events, and old music clips. I do not post every day, but I might share a birthday message, a Red Sox comment, or a picture of tomatoes from the garden. I use video calls more than social media for real conversation. I do not use Instagram much and I am not on TikTok. I try not to get pulled into arguments because online people say things they would not say at a kitchen table.

follow_ups.question: Who helped you learn Facebook?
follow_ups.response: My granddaughter Sofia set it up and showed me how not to accept every friend request.

follow_ups.question: Do you follow news there?
follow_ups.response: Only lightly; I prefer local news sites, TV, and official pages.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?
transcript.response: I do not ask for financial support online. For emotional support, I may post a prayer request or respond to one, but real support comes through phone calls, church, and family.

follow_ups.question: Have you donated to online fundraisers?
follow_ups.response: A couple times for people I actually know, like medical or funeral costs.

follow_ups.question: Would you post if you needed help?
follow_ups.response: Probably not first; I would talk to family privately.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your level of stress, worry, and your emotional coping strategies.
transcript.response: My stress is more about aging and health than work now. I cope better than before by walking, praying, calling people, and stepping away from news when it gets too much.

follow_ups.question: Has retirement lowered stress?
follow_ups.response: Yes for work pressure, no for medical and money paperwork.

follow_ups.question: What coping habit are you trying to improve?
follow_ups.response: I am trying to talk before I get cranky, instead of pretending I am fine.

transcript.question_text: This might be repetitive, but before we go on to the next section, I want to quickly make sure I have this right: who are you living with right now?
transcript.response: I live with my wife, Maria Gonzalez, in our home in Taunton. No one else lives with us full time.

follow_ups.question: Just the two of you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, just the two of us.

follow_ups.question: Are both of you there year-round?
follow_ups.response: Yes, except for short visits or trips.

transcript.question_text: Any babies or small children?
transcript.response: No babies or small children live here.

follow_ups.question: Do small children visit?
follow_ups.response: Yes, younger relatives visit for family gatherings.

follow_ups.question: Any regular childcare here?
follow_ups.response: No regular childcare.

transcript.question_text: Anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody is away.

follow_ups.question: No one away temporarily?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: No college student listed here?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Any lodgers, boarders, or employees who live here?
transcript.response: No, none.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever rented a room?
follow_ups.response: No, we have not.

follow_ups.question: Any live-in help?
follow_ups.response: No live-in help.

transcript.question_text: Who shares the responsibility for the rent, mortgage, or other household expenses?
transcript.response: Maria and I share household expenses from my pension, Social Security, and our savings.

follow_ups.question: Is there still a mortgage?
follow_ups.response: No regular mortgage; the main housing costs are taxes, insurance, utilities, and repairs.

follow_ups.question: Do children contribute?
follow_ups.response: Not regularly, only if there is a special need.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to talk about how you make ends meet and what the monthly budget looks like for you and your family. What were your biggest expenses last month?
transcript.response: Last month the biggest expenses were property taxes set aside, utilities, groceries, insurance, prescriptions, and a car repair. Groceries are higher than they used to be, especially meat, coffee, and fresh produce when the garden is not producing.

follow_ups.question: What was the car repair?
follow_ups.response: Brakes and inspection on our older Toyota.

follow_ups.question: Do you track expenses closely?
follow_ups.response: Maria tracks them closely, and I keep receipts when I remember.

transcript.question_text: How much did your household spend in the past month? Is that the usual amount? And if not, how much do you usually spend and on what?
transcript.response: Last month was around $3,700 because of the car repair. A more normal month is closer to $3,100 to $3,300 for utilities, food, insurance, medical costs, gas, church giving, and home supplies.

follow_ups.question: What category has risen most?
follow_ups.response: Groceries and utilities, especially heating in winter.

follow_ups.question: Do you use credit cards for monthly expenses?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but we try to pay them off each month.

transcript.question_text: Does your household own or rent your home?
transcript.response: We own our home in Taunton. The mortgage is paid off, which is a blessing, but owning still means taxes, insurance, heating, repairs, and everything that breaks becoming my problem.

follow_ups.question: When did you buy the house?
follow_ups.response: In the early 1980s.

follow_ups.question: What made you choose it?
follow_ups.response: It had a yard, a garage, enough bedrooms for the kids, and a price we could manage.

transcript.question_text: Bills can fluctuate over the course of a year. Seasons change, there are holidays and special events, school starts and ends, and so on. Tell me all about how your bills have fluctuated over the past year.
transcript.response: Winter heating is the biggest swing, and summer brings yard supplies, garden things, and sometimes higher water use. Holidays cost more because we cook for family and buy gifts for grandchildren. Insurance and property tax bills come in chunks, so Maria plans ahead for those.

follow_ups.question: Which holiday costs most?
follow_ups.response: Christmas and Three Kings Day together, because food and gifts stretch across both.

follow_ups.question: Do summer bills feel easier?
follow_ups.response: A little, because heat is off, but then house projects appear.

transcript.question_text: Tell me all about how you coped with any extra expenses in the past months.
transcript.response: We used savings for the car repair and delayed buying new lumber for a woodworking project. I also fixed a small plumbing issue myself instead of calling someone.

follow_ups.question: Do you cut back on groceries?
follow_ups.response: Not necessities, but we buy sales, cook more beans and rice, and waste less.

follow_ups.question: Do you ask family for help?
follow_ups.response: Not unless it is serious.

transcript.question_text: Some people have a savings account, some people save in a different way, and some people say they don't save. How about you?
transcript.response: We have a savings account and a small retirement cushion. We are not rich, but we always tried to keep something aside because machines break, cars break, and bodies break. Maria is better at saving than I am; I can convince myself a new tool is necessary. We also save informally by keeping the house maintained so problems do not become disasters.

follow_ups.question: Who manages savings decisions?
follow_ups.response: Maria manages the accounts, and we talk before bigger withdrawals.

follow_ups.question: What counts as a big purchase?
follow_ups.response: Anything over a few hundred dollars, especially appliances, travel, or major repairs.

transcript.question_text: Some people save for big things, like a home, while others save for a rainy day. How about for you (in the last year)?
transcript.response: This past year we saved mostly for rainy day needs: medical costs, house repairs, and maybe a Puerto Rico trip if our health lines up. At our age, saving is less about buying something impressive and more about not becoming a burden. I would like to take Maria to Puerto Rico comfortably, with a decent hotel and no rushing. That takes planning.

follow_ups.question: How much planning would the Puerto Rico trip need?
follow_ups.response: Flights, accessible lodging, relatives' schedules, medicines, and enough rest days between visits.

follow_ups.question: What emergency worries you most?
follow_ups.response: A major home repair like heating system trouble or a medical bill.

transcript.question_text: Some people have student loans or credit card debt. Others take out loans from family or friends or find other ways of borrowing money. Tell me about all the debts you're paying on right now.
transcript.response: We do not have student loans or a mortgage. We have a credit card balance sometimes during the month, but we try to pay it off. The car is paid for, so our debt is low right now.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever carried credit card debt?
follow_ups.response: Yes, when the kids were younger and the house needed repairs, but we worked it down.

follow_ups.question: Do you lend money to family?
follow_ups.response: Small amounts sometimes, but I prefer helping with groceries or repairs.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any time during the past year that you haven't had enough money to buy something that you needed or pay a bill that was due.
transcript.response: We have not missed a bill this past year. There were times we postponed things, like dental work or buying materials, because I did not like the price. I know that is different from truly not having enough. We are careful because fixed income means a few bad surprises can change the month fast.

follow_ups.question: What did you postpone?
follow_ups.response: Some dental work timing and a larger woodworking project.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel financially secure?
follow_ups.response: Mostly secure, but not careless.

transcript.question_text: What is or was your occupation? In this occupation, what kind of work do you do and what are the most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: I was a maintenance mechanic in manufacturing for almost forty years. My job was to keep the plant running: repair conveyor belts, pumps, motors, gearboxes, valves, electrical controls, and sometimes plumbing or compressed air lines. Preventive maintenance was important because a small vibration could become a shutdown if you ignored it. I read manuals, listened to operators, traced problems, welded small parts sometimes, and worked with electricians when controls were involved. The most important duty was safety, because a machine does not forgive you if you get careless.

follow_ups.question: What kind of plant was it?
follow_ups.response: A manufacturing plant in the Greater Boston area that made and packaged industrial components and materials for other businesses.

follow_ups.question: What skill were you best known for?
follow_ups.response: Troubleshooting stubborn mechanical problems and making a repair hold without overcomplicating it.

transcript.question_text: Was your occupation covered by a union or employee association contract?
transcript.response: Yes, for much of my career I was covered by a union contract. It helped with wages, overtime rules, safety, and retirement benefits.

follow_ups.question: Were you active in the union?
follow_ups.response: I was not an officer, but I went to meetings when important votes came up.

follow_ups.question: Did the union matter to your family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it gave us stability and benefits I did not fully appreciate until later.

transcript.question_text: In the past year, how many weeks did you work (for a few hours, including paid vacation, paid sick leave, and military service)?
transcript.response: Zero weeks for paid work. I am retired and not in the workforce.

follow_ups.question: Any unpaid work?
follow_ups.response: Plenty, but it is home, family, church, and neighbor help.

follow_ups.question: When did you retire?
follow_ups.response: I retired in 2013.

transcript.question_text: How many hours each week did you usually work?
transcript.response: Now, zero paid hours. When I was working, it was usually forty hours, with overtime when machines broke.

follow_ups.question: How much overtime was common?
follow_ups.response: Some weeks five to ten hours, more during shutdowns.

follow_ups.question: What shift did you prefer?
follow_ups.response: Day shift, because it let me be home for dinner.

transcript.question_text: In the past week, did you work for pay (even for 1 hour) at a job or business?
transcript.response: No, I did not work for pay in the past week.

follow_ups.question: Any paid side job?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Any business income?
follow_ups.response: No business income.

transcript.question_text: Did you have more than one job or business, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: No, not now. Earlier in life I sometimes did small weekend repair help, but not as a formal second job.

follow_ups.question: Were those repairs paid?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes cash, sometimes favors, but nothing regular.

follow_ups.question: Would you take that on now?
follow_ups.response: No, only light help for people I know.

transcript.question_text: Now, in the past month, how many jobs did you work, including part time, evening, or weekend work?
transcript.response: None. I worked no paid jobs in the past month.

follow_ups.question: Any volunteer role counted as work?
follow_ups.response: No formal volunteer job, just occasional help.

follow_ups.question: Any job search?
follow_ups.response: No, I am retired.

transcript.question_text: For your job or occupations, how much money did you receive in the past month?
transcript.response: From jobs, zero dollars. Our income comes from Social Security, my pension, and a smaller Social Security benefit for Maria.

follow_ups.question: Do you receive pension income monthly?
follow_ups.response: Yes, my pension comes monthly.

follow_ups.question: Any cash from woodworking?
follow_ups.response: No, I give pieces to family or make things for the house.

transcript.question_text: How often do you get paid?
transcript.response: My pension and Social Security come monthly.

follow_ups.question: Is the timing predictable?
follow_ups.response: Yes, predictable enough that Maria plans bills around it.

follow_ups.question: Any weekly income?
follow_ups.response: No weekly income.

transcript.question_text: In total, how much did your household make in the past month?
transcript.response: Together, before deductions, around $4,600 in a typical month from pension and Social Security. It varies little, which is good for planning but tight when costs rise.

follow_ups.question: Is that after taxes?
follow_ups.response: That is roughly before some deductions and supplemental insurance costs.

follow_ups.question: Does anyone else contribute income?
follow_ups.response: No regular contribution.

transcript.question_text: Switching gears a bit, let's talk a little about tax time. Did you file taxes last year (the most recent year)?
transcript.response: Yes, we filed taxes last year. We use a local tax preparer because pensions, Social Security, and medical deductions are easier when someone who knows the forms handles it.

follow_ups.question: Do you usually get a refund?
follow_ups.response: Usually small, nothing dramatic.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep records through the year?
follow_ups.response: Maria keeps folders with tax papers, medical expenses, and donation receipts.

transcript.question_text: Tell me more about your workplace. How long have you been at your current job? How would you describe the benefits that come with your job? (This could include things like health benefits, paid time off, vacation, and sick time.)
transcript.response: I do not have a current job. In my plant job, I worked nearly forty years and had health insurance, vacation, sick time, and pension benefits through the union contract.

follow_ups.question: Were benefits important to staying?
follow_ups.response: Very important, especially once we had children.

follow_ups.question: Did benefits change over time?
follow_ups.response: Yes, health costs rose and negotiations got harder.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your relationships at work? (How is your relationship with your manager or boss? How are your relationships with your coworkers?)
transcript.response: When I worked, I got along with most coworkers and had respectful but sometimes tense relationships with managers, especially during breakdowns.

follow_ups.question: Do you still see coworkers?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a few for coffee, wakes, fishing, or phone calls.

follow_ups.question: What caused tension with managers?
follow_ups.response: Production wanted speed, but maintenance needed safe repairs.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about how predictable your work schedule is. How would you describe your job in terms of flexibility with your hours?
transcript.response: My current schedule is flexible because I am retired. My old work schedule was mostly predictable day shift, but breakdowns changed everything. If a line went down near quitting time, you stayed. Shutdown weeks could mean long days. The union helped keep overtime fair, but machinery does not care about your dinner plans.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect family life?
follow_ups.response: Yes, Maria had to handle many evenings when I got stuck at work.

follow_ups.question: Do you enjoy flexibility now?
follow_ups.response: Yes, though too much flexibility can make me disorganized.

transcript.question_text: Some people say it's hard to take or keep a job because of child care. How about for you?
transcript.response: When the children were young, Maria carried much of the child care load, and relatives helped. It was not the reason I left work, but it was always part of family planning.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever miss work for children?
follow_ups.response: Yes, for sickness or school emergencies, but Maria handled more.

follow_ups.question: What about now?
follow_ups.response: Now child care is not an employment issue for me.

transcript.question_text: Do you receive any payments or benefits from SNAP, food stamps, housing voucher payments, supplemental security income, or any other programs like that?
transcript.response: No SNAP, housing voucher, or SSI. We receive Social Security and Medicare, and I receive a pension.

follow_ups.question: Any veterans benefits?
follow_ups.response: No, I did not serve.

follow_ups.question: Any fuel assistance?
follow_ups.response: No, not currently.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about times over the last year when your income was especially low. And tell me about all the things you did to make ends meet during that time.
transcript.response: Our income did not drop much because it is fixed monthly. The problem is prices going up while income stays nearly the same. We coped by using savings carefully, delaying projects, cooking at home, watching sales, and doing repairs ourselves.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel fixed income is predictable or limiting?
follow_ups.response: Both; predictable for bills, limiting when everything costs more.

follow_ups.question: What do you refuse to cut?
follow_ups.response: Medicine, decent food, church giving, and family meals.

transcript.question_text: What would it be like for you if you had to spend $400 for an emergency? Would you have the money, and if not, how would you get it?
transcript.response: We could handle a $400 emergency from savings, though I would not be happy about it. If several emergencies came together, then we would use a credit card temporarily or ask the children for help.

follow_ups.question: What kind of emergency do you imagine?
follow_ups.response: Car repair, plumbing leak, prescription issue, or appliance failure.

follow_ups.question: Would it change the monthly budget?
follow_ups.response: Yes, we would cut extras that month.

transcript.question_text: Overall, how do you feel about your financial situation?
transcript.response: I feel stable but cautious. We own the house, have monthly income, and are not drowning in debt, so I know we are fortunate. But I also know one serious medical problem or house repair can eat savings fast. I do not feel poor, but I do not feel like I can ignore prices. My goal is to stay independent and not make my children carry us financially.

follow_ups.question: What financial decision are you proudest of?
follow_ups.response: Buying the house and staying with the job long enough to earn a pension.

follow_ups.question: What do you wish you had done differently?
follow_ups.response: Saved more earlier and learned investing beyond basic retirement choices.

transcript.question_text: Are you now married, widowed, divorced, separated, or have you never been married? If you are not currently married, are you currently living with a romantic partner?
transcript.response: I am currently married to Maria, and we live together.

follow_ups.question: How long have you been married?
follow_ups.response: Over fifty years.

follow_ups.question: Were you ever previously married?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.response: My date of birth is March 14, 1949.

follow_ups.response: Yes, seventy-seven.

follow_ups.question: Do you celebrate birthdays with family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, usually dinner and cake at the house.

transcript.question_text: Were you born in the United States? If you were not born in the U.S., what country were you born, and what year did you first come to the U.S. to live?
transcript.response: I was born in Puerto Rico, a U.S. territory, and came to the mainland United States as a child in 1956.

follow_ups.question: How old were you then?
follow_ups.response: About seven years old.

follow_ups.question: Do you remember the move?
follow_ups.response: I remember the cold and my mother worrying about coats.

transcript.question_text: What city and state were you born in?
transcript.response: I was born in Ponce, Puerto Rico.

follow_ups.question: Do you still have family there?
follow_ups.response: Yes, cousins and extended family.

follow_ups.question: Have you visited as an adult?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but not as often as I would like.

transcript.response: Yes, I am Hispanic, Puerto Rican.

follow_ups.question: What term do you use most?
follow_ups.response: Puerto Rican.

follow_ups.question: Do you speak Spanish?
follow_ups.response: Yes, Spanish and English.

transcript.question_text: What race or races do you identify with?
transcript.response: I usually identify as White Hispanic or multiracial Puerto Rican, with Spanish, Taino, and Afro-Caribbean roots in the family.

follow_ups.question: Is that easy to mark on forms?
follow_ups.response: Not always; forms do not always fit Puerto Rican history well.

follow_ups.question: What identity feels most important?
follow_ups.response: Puerto Rican and American together.

transcript.question_text: What is the highest degree or grade you've completed?

follow_ups.response: Mostly on-the-job training and plant courses, not a degree.

follow_ups.question: Did you enjoy school?
follow_ups.response: Some parts, especially history and shop.

transcript.response: No, I am not enrolled in school.

follow_ups.response: Only occasional senior center workshops.

follow_ups.response: Maybe genealogy or computer basics.

transcript.response: No, I have not been enrolled in school during the past three months.

follow_ups.question: Any formal training recently?
follow_ups.response: No formal training.

follow_ups.question: Any informal learning?
follow_ups.response: Yes, online genealogy and woodworking videos.

transcript.question_text: Have you ever served on active duty in the U.S. Armed Forces, Reserves, or National Guard?
transcript.response: No, I have never served in the U.S. Armed Forces, Reserves, or National Guard.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever consider it?
follow_ups.response: Briefly when I was young, but I chose work instead.

follow_ups.question: Any veterans in your family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, some cousins served.

transcript.question_text: What religion do you identify with, if any?
transcript.response: I identify as Roman Catholic.

follow_ups.question: Do you actively practice?
follow_ups.response: Yes, Mass most Sundays and prayer at home.

follow_ups.response: Yes, very much so.

transcript.question_text: Generally speaking, do you usually think of yourself as a Democrat, a Republican, an Independent, or what? And how strongly do you associate with that party?
transcript.response: I usually think of myself as a Democrat, but not blindly. I would say moderately strong, because the Democratic Party has been closer to labor, seniors, health care, and immigrant families in my lifetime. I have voted for local candidates based on the person, but nationally I lean Democratic. I do not like extreme talk from either side.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever voted Republican?
follow_ups.response: For a local office maybe once or twice, if I trusted the person.

follow_ups.question: Do you donate to campaigns?
follow_ups.response: Rarely; maybe a small amount, but not often.

transcript.question_text: Do you think of yourself as closer to the Democratic Party or to the Republican Party?
transcript.response: Closer to the Democratic Party. I may disagree with some Democrats, but on working families, Medicare, unions, and respect for immigrants, that is where I fit better.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you from calling yourself independent?
follow_ups.response: My voting pattern and values line up Democratic more often.

follow_ups.question: What frustrates you about Democrats?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes they talk too much in fancy language and forget practical people.

transcript.question_text: What was the city and state that you lived in when you were 16 years old?
transcript.response: When I was sixteen, I lived in Boston, Massachusetts, in a neighborhood with many working immigrant families.

follow_ups.question: Which part of Boston?
follow_ups.response: Mostly the South End/Roxbury area as it was changing then.

follow_ups.question: Did you like it there?
follow_ups.response: It was crowded and sometimes rough, but full of family and life.

transcript.question_text: Did you live with both your own mother and father when you were 16?
transcript.response: Yes, I lived with both my mother and father when I was sixteen.

follow_ups.question: Were they strict?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially about school, church, respect, and coming home on time.

follow_ups.question: Did they speak English?
follow_ups.response: Some, but Spanish was the language of the home.

transcript.question_text: Who else did you live with?
transcript.response: I lived with my younger sister Isabel, my brother Rafael, and for a while an aunt stayed with us too.

follow_ups.question: Was the home crowded?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but that was normal for us then.

follow_ups.question: Did extended family visit often?
follow_ups.response: Constantly; cousins and compadres were always around.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your dad completed?
transcript.response: My father completed around sixth grade in Puerto Rico.

follow_ups.question: Could he read and write?
follow_ups.response: Yes, in Spanish, and he learned practical English over time.

follow_ups.question: Did he value education?
follow_ups.response: Very much, because he knew what limited schooling cost him.

transcript.question_text: What's the highest degree or grade your mom completed?
transcript.response: My mother completed about eighth grade.

follow_ups.question: Was she proud of your diploma?
follow_ups.response: Very proud; she treated it like a family achievement.

follow_ups.question: Did she help with schoolwork?
follow_ups.response: She helped by enforcing discipline more than by helping with English homework.

transcript.question_text: Did your mom work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, my mother worked for pay for several years while I was growing up.

follow_ups.question: Did she also manage the home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, she worked and still carried most of the cooking and household load.

follow_ups.question: Was that common in your neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: Yes, many mothers worked in factories, cleaning, sewing, or kitchens.

transcript.question_text: What was her job? What kind of work did she do? What were her most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My mother worked in garment sewing and later in a hospital laundry. She stitched, sorted, folded, and kept up with fast production demands. Her most important duties were accuracy, speed, and not complaining even when her hands hurt.

follow_ups.question: Did she like the work?
follow_ups.response: She liked earning money but it was hard work, not a dream job.

follow_ups.question: What did you learn from her work?
follow_ups.response: Endurance, pride, and that invisible work still holds families together.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did she work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where she worked?
transcript.response: The garment place made clothing and did piecework, and the hospital laundry cleaned linens, gowns, and uniforms. These were busy, practical workplaces where immigrant women did much of the labor. She came home tired, smelling like soap or fabric dust.

follow_ups.question: Was it union work?
follow_ups.response: I do not think so, not in the way my later plant job was.

follow_ups.question: Did language matter there?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but many workers spoke Spanish, Portuguese, or other languages, so people helped each other.

transcript.question_text: Did your dad work for pay for at least a year while you were growing up?
transcript.response: Yes, my father worked for pay the whole time I was growing up.

follow_ups.question: Was he ever unemployed?
follow_ups.response: Short stretches, but he always looked for work quickly.

follow_ups.question: Did he work long hours?
follow_ups.response: Yes, and sometimes weekends.

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My father worked in factory and warehouse jobs, mostly machine operation, loading, and maintenance helper work. He moved materials, watched machines, cleaned equipment, and fixed simple problems when he could. His duties were physical, repetitive, and demanding, but he took pride in being reliable.

follow_ups.question: Did his work influence your career?
follow_ups.response: Yes, seeing him fix things and respect tools pushed me toward maintenance.

follow_ups.question: What was he like after work?
follow_ups.response: Tired, quiet at first, then warmer after dinner and coffee.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked in industrial shops and warehouses around Boston that handled manufactured goods, packaging, and supplies. They were noisy places with forklifts, loading docks, and machines that always needed attention. He did not have a fancy title, but he helped keep goods moving.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever visit his workplace?
follow_ups.response: Once or twice from outside, and I remember the noise and smell.

follow_ups.question: What did he want for you?
follow_ups.response: He wanted me to have steadier work, safer work, and better English than he had.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope Maria and I are still in this house, still able to go to Mass, cook, and sit in the yard. I hope my health stays good enough to travel to Puerto Rico one more time and visit family without rushing. I want to finish the family memoir with photos, recipes, and stories of how my parents came here. I hope to keep teaching the grandchildren things that do not come from a phone: how to sharpen a chisel, make sofrito, plant tomatoes, shake a hand, and keep your word. I also hope the neighborhood still sees me as useful, not just old.

follow_ups.question: What would make the next few years feel successful?
follow_ups.response: Staying independent, finishing the memoir, making that Puerto Rico trip, and seeing the grandchildren moving in good directions.

follow_ups.question: What worries you about the future?
follow_ups.response: Mobility, medical costs, and leaving too many stories untold.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value family, faith, health, honest work, and keeping your culture alive. Money matters because bills are real, but money is not the thing people remember at your table. They remember whether you showed up, whether you fed them, whether your word meant something. I value being useful, telling the truth, and leaving my grandchildren with roots strong enough that they know who they are.

follow_ups.question: What value did your parents give you most strongly?
follow_ups.response: Hard work with dignity.

follow_ups.question: What value do you most want grandchildren to carry?
follow_ups.response: Respect your family and heritage, but also learn enough to stand on your own feet.

summaries.demographer: Antonio Gonzalez is a 77-year-old married Puerto Rican/Hispanic man living with his wife Maria in an owner-occupied home in Taunton, Massachusetts (Q51, Q58, Q84, Q88). He was born in Ponce, Puerto Rico, came to the mainland United States as a child in 1956, lived in Boston at age sixteen, and completed high school (Q86, Q87, Q90, Q97). He is retired from a long union-covered career as a maintenance mechanic and now relies on Social Security, pension income, Medicare, and savings (Q65, Q66, Q74, Q80). His household is an older two-person empty-nest household with nearby adult children, grandchildren, siblings, church ties, and neighborhood supports (Q05-Q07, Q11).
summaries.behavioral_economist: Antonio shows strong loss aversion and precautionary planning: he owns his home, avoids debt, maintains savings for emergencies, delays discretionary spending, and uses self-repair to reduce costs (Q58, Q60-Q64, Q82). His choices are motivated by family duty, independence, cultural continuity, and practical usefulness rather than consumption status (Q05, Q83, Q108, Q109). He responds well to social accountability, as shown by walking group participation for diabetes control and weekly dominoes for social engagement (Q07, Q18, Q32). He is cautious about risk, preferring predictable income, planned travel, trusted medical sources, and low-stress routines (Q42, Q62, Q74).
summaries.political_scientist: Antonio is a regular voter and moderately strong Democrat with a pro-labor, pro-Medicare, pro-Social Security orientation rooted in his working-class union career and immigrant-family experience (Q23, Q24, Q66, Q95). He supports government help for seniors, workers, public schools, and people facing unfair treatment, while remaining fiscally practical as a homeowner on fixed income (Q24, Q56-Q59). He views Black Lives Matter and race-related policing debates as raising real accountability concerns, filtered through his experience as a Puerto Rican man who faced suspicion and language barriers (Q20, Q26-Q30). His civic life is local and relational: voting, church, senior center networks, neighborhood repair help, and community listening matter more than partisan activism (Q17, Q23, Q47).
summaries.psychologist: Antonio presents as conscientious, practical, family-centered, competitive in friendly settings, and identity-driven around competence and usefulness (Q01, Q07, Q65, Q109). He copes with aging, grief, and worry through activity, prayer, music, repair work, family conversation, and structured routines rather than formal mental health care (Q38, Q43-Q45, Q50). His self-concept is anchored in being a reliable husband, father, grandfather, craftsman, Catholic, Puerto Rican storyteller, and neighborhood helper (Q05, Q16, Q47, Q108). He is emotionally restrained but increasingly reflective, especially about mortality, legacy, and the need to preserve family stories before they are lost (Q43, Q44, Q108).
